statement: Security requirements and risks are addressed at defined stages of every project, whatever its type. The project management method names those stages, and each project keeps a security risk assessment or a requirements sign-off. This catches security problems while they are cheap to fix. Proof is the project method and the project records.
why_asked: Security added at the end of a project is costly and often skipped for non-software projects. Consultants check the method requires it for all project types and that real projects show it.
how_to_ask: Ask how a new project, including a non-software one, triggers a security review and who signs off. Example probe: "Show me the security sign-off from the last project that went live."
question: Does your organization require security requirements and risks to be addressed at defined stages of every project?
expected_evidence: Project management method showing security stages and gates; project records with security risk assessments; gate sign-off records. Cover projects completed or started in the last audit period.
good_looks_like: The project method requires security requirements and risk review at named stages for every project type. Sampled projects hold a dated risk assessment or sign-off from a named approver.
test: Read the project method for required security stages. Sample projects from the period, including a non-software one if any, and look for the assessment or sign-off at each required stage. Pass if every sampled project shows the required security record.
baseline_risk: Projects launch with unaddressed security risks that are expensive or impossible to fix later.

statement: Security rules are set for each phase of the development life cycle: requirements, design, coding, testing and release. Release records show the required security steps were completed, such as a security review, a code scan or an approval gate. This builds security into every release instead of checking it at the end. Proof is the secure development policy and the release records.
why_asked: A policy that is not visible in release records is not being followed. Consultants test sampled releases against the required steps.
how_to_ask: Ask what steps a release must pass and how the organization prevents a release from skipping them. Example probe: "Show me the last release and the evidence that each required security step was done."
question: Does your organization set security rules for each phase of development and show that releases follow them?
expected_evidence: Secure development policy by life-cycle phase; release records with completed security steps; scan results; approval gate records. Cover releases from the last audit period.
good_looks_like: A policy defines security rules for each phase. Release records and pipeline gates show review, scanning and approval completed before release, and skipped steps need an approved exception.
test: Read the policy for the required steps per phase. Sample releases from the period and check each for evidence of every required step. Pass if every sampled release shows the steps completed or an approved exception.
baseline_risk: Releases ship with security flaws because required steps are skipped or never defined.
applicability: Applies if the organization develops software in house or has it developed for it.

statement: Security requirements are identified, specified and approved whenever an application is built or acquired, including software as a service. Each application keeps a documented, approved set of requirements. This makes sure applications fit the organization's security needs before purchase or build. Proof is the requirements records and the approvals.
why_asked: Applications bought or built without stated security needs end up with gaps nobody planned for. Consultants test acquired and SaaS applications as well as in-house ones.
how_to_ask: Ask how security needs are captured for a new application and who approves them. Example probe: "Show me the approved security requirements for the last application you bought or built."
question: Does your organization identify, specify and approve security requirements for the applications it builds or buys?
expected_evidence: Development and procurement process steps requiring security requirements; approved requirements documents for sampled applications; approval records. Cover applications started in the last audit period.
good_looks_like: Both the build and the buy processes require a documented requirements set before approval. Sampled applications, including SaaS, show requirements and a named approver.
test: Read the development and procurement process for the requirements step. Sample applications built or acquired in the period and look for a documented, approved requirements set. Pass if every sampled application has one approved before go-live.
baseline_risk: Applications are adopted without stated security needs and leave unaddressed gaps.

statement: Principles for engineering secure systems, such as defense in depth, least privilege, secure defaults and zero trust, are documented and kept current. They are applied in design and architecture reviews, and the review records show it. This gives development work a common bar for secure design.
why_asked: Principles on a page do nothing unless design reviews use them. Consultants check that reviews cite the principles.
how_to_ask: Ask where the principles are written and how architects use them in reviews. Example probe: "Show me a recent design review and where it applied one of your principles."
question: Does your organization apply documented secure engineering principles in its system and application design?
expected_evidence: Secure engineering principles document with version history; architecture or design review records; review checklists. Cover reviews in the last audit period.
good_looks_like: Principles are written, versioned and reviewed on a defined cycle. Design reviews for sampled development work record which principles were applied and any exceptions.
test: Read the principles and confirm they are current. Sample design or architecture reviews from the period and look for recorded application of the principles. Pass if sampled reviews record the principles were applied or document exceptions.
baseline_risk: Systems are designed inconsistently and carry avoidable structural weaknesses.
applicability: Applies if the organization develops software in house or has it developed for it.

statement: A secure coding standard covers input validation, output encoding, secrets handling and dependency management, and applies to in-house and outsourced code. Code changes go through peer review or automated scanning, such as static analysis, dependency or secret scanning, and findings are addressed before release. This keeps common coding flaws out of production. Proof is the standard and the pipeline scan results.
why_asked: Common flaws like injection and exposed secrets reach production when nothing checks code changes. Consultants look for a standard and for scan or review evidence on real changes.
how_to_ask: Ask what the standard covers, which checks run on every change and whether findings can block a release. Example probe: "Show me a recent change where a scan finding was fixed before release."
question: Does your organization apply a secure coding standard and check code changes by review or automated scanning before release?
expected_evidence: Secure coding standard; pipeline configuration showing scans; scan results and peer review records for sampled changes; finding resolution records. Cover changes in the last audit period.
good_looks_like: A secure coding standard covers in-house and outsourced code. The pipeline runs review or scans on every change, and findings are fixed or accepted with approval before release.
test: Read the standard and the pipeline configuration. Sample code changes released in the period and check each for a review or scan record and resolved findings. Pass if sampled changes show checks done and findings addressed before release.
baseline_risk: Preventable coding flaws and leaked secrets reach production and are exploited.
applicability: Applies if the organization develops software in house or has it developed for it.

statement: The security tests required at each stage of development, and the acceptance criteria that must be met before go-live, are defined. For new or significantly changed systems, test results and an acceptance sign-off are kept before production release. This confirms a system is safe to run before it handles real data. Proof is the test process and the test and acceptance records.
why_asked: Systems that go live without defined tests or sign-off carry unknown risk. Consultants test that results and a sign-off exist before release, not after.
how_to_ask: Ask what tests are required, who accepts results and who can stop a release. Example probe: "Show me the acceptance sign-off for your last major release and the test results behind it."
question: Does your organization require security testing and sign-off before each release?
expected_evidence: Security testing process with stage tests and acceptance criteria; test reports; acceptance sign-off records for new or changed systems. Cover releases in the last audit period.
good_looks_like: A process lists the tests per stage and clear acceptance criteria. Each significant release shows test results and a dated sign-off by a named approver before production.
test: Read the process for tests and criteria. Sample new or significantly changed systems released in the period and check for test results and a sign-off dated before release. Pass if every sampled system has both and meets the acceptance criteria.
baseline_risk: Systems reach production with undiscovered flaws because no one confirmed they met security criteria.

statement: Contracts for outsourced development set security requirements, such as secure coding, test evidence, code ownership and a right to audit. The outsourced work is monitored and reviewed, for example through code reviews, test evidence received and progress meetings, and records are kept. This keeps outsourced code to the same standard as in-house code.
why_asked: Outsourced developers can introduce flaws or backdoors the organization never sees. Consultants check both the contract terms and proof of oversight.
how_to_ask: Ask who develops software for the organization, what their contracts require and how the work is checked. Example probe: "Show me the last test evidence or code review you received from your outside developers."
question: Does your organization oversee the security of outsourced development?
expected_evidence: Outsourced development contracts with security terms; oversight records such as code review, test evidence and meeting minutes; supplier performance reviews. Cover the last audit period.
good_looks_like: Contracts require secure coding, testing evidence, ownership and audit rights. Oversight records show the organization reviewed delivered work and acted on issues.
test: List outsourced development suppliers and sample some. Check each contract for the security terms and look for oversight records from the period. Pass if sampled contracts include the terms and records show reviews of delivered work.
baseline_risk: Outsourced code arrives with flaws or hidden access, and the organization cannot prove what it received.
applicability: Applies if the organization outsources software development.

statement: Development, test and production environments are separate, for example in separate accounts, subscriptions or networks, with rules for promoting changes between them. Developers have no standing write access to production, or any such access is approved and logged. Non-production environments are secured to the level of the data they hold. Proof is the separation rules and the access configuration.
why_asked: Shared environments let test mistakes hit production and let developers change live data unseen. Consultants check access settings, not only the design.
how_to_ask: Ask how environments are separated, who can write to production and how test environments are protected. Example probe: "Show me which developers can change production today and why."
question: Does your organization keep its development, test and production environments separate?
expected_evidence: Environment separation rules; cloud or system access export showing developer rights in production; approval and log records for any production access; non-production security settings. Cover the current configuration and the last audit period.
good_looks_like: Environments are in separate accounts or networks with documented promotion rules. Developers lack standing production write access, any exception is approved and logged, and non-production matches the protection of the data it holds.
test: Read the separation rules. Inspect the access export for developer rights in production and sample non-production environments for access control and data protection. Pass if developers lack standing write access or have approved logged access, and non-production security fits its data.
baseline_risk: Test activity or developer changes damage production, and weakly protected test systems leak real data.
applicability: Applies if the organization develops software in house or has it developed for it.

statement: A change procedure for systems and facilities covers recording, impact and risk assessment, authorization, testing, rollback planning and communication. Each change is assessed for cybersecurity risk impact before approval and tracked to closure. Production changes are authorized before they are made, with testing evidence kept. Emergency changes are recorded and reviewed and approved afterward. Unintended changes are reviewed for their effect, and any harm is dealt with. This keeps changes from causing outages or security gaps. Proof is the procedure and the change records.
why_asked: Uncontrolled changes are a leading cause of outages and security regressions. Consultants test authorization timing and the handling of emergency changes.
how_to_ask: Ask how a change is requested, approved and tested, and what happens when something must change in an emergency. Example probe: "Show me your last emergency change and its after-the-fact approval."
question: Does your organization put changes to its systems through recorded assessment, authorization, testing and rollback planning?
expected_evidence: Change management procedure; change records with approval and test evidence; emergency change records with retrospective approval. Cover changes in the last audit period.
good_looks_like: A procedure covers every step from recording to communication. Sampled changes show a risk assessment and approval before implementation, testing evidence and closure, and emergency changes are recorded and approved afterward. Unintended changes found in the period have a recorded review and follow-up.
test: Read the procedure for the required steps. Sample production changes from the period and check a cybersecurity risk assessment was recorded before approval, authorization precedes implementation, testing evidence exists and the change was tracked to closure, then check emergency changes for retrospective approval and any unintended changes for a recorded review of their effect. Pass if all sampled changes meet these conditions.
baseline_risk: Unauthorized or untested changes cause outages, data loss or new vulnerabilities.

statement: Rules for selecting and using test data require production or personal data to be masked or explicitly authorized before it is used in testing. Any copy of production data into a test environment has an authorization record and is deleted after testing. This keeps real data out of weakly protected test systems. Proof is the test data rules and the authorization and deletion records.
why_asked: Real customer data copied to test systems is easily exposed and often forgotten there. Consultants look for authorization and proof of deletion.
how_to_ask: Ask how test data is created, whether real data is ever copied and who approves it. Example probe: "When did you last copy production data to test, who approved it and when was it deleted?"
question: Does your organization prevent production or personal data from being used in testing without approval?
expected_evidence: Test data rules; masking or synthetic data approach; authorization records for production data copies; deletion confirmations. Cover copies made in the last audit period.
good_looks_like: Rules require masked or synthetic data by default. Any production copy has an approval, a stated purpose and a recorded deletion after testing.
test: Read the rules. List production data copies to test environments in the period and sample them. Pass if each sampled copy has an authorization record and evidence it was deleted after testing, or the organization shows none occurred.
baseline_risk: Real or personal data sits in weakly protected test environments and is exposed.
applicability: Applies if the organization develops software in house or has it developed for it.
